title: The Asian monsoon system
summary: A high-resolution climate record from 27.32 to 23.24 million years ago shows that the South Asian monsoon had already reached central Tibet in the late Oligocene. Work on the Lunpola Basin during 26 to 16 million years ago highlights how the shape of the land and long-period changes in Earth's orbit drove the monsoon's evolution over tectonic time.

uncertainty.note: Paleoclimatic pollen and cyclostratigraphic records from central Tibet bracket the intensification of the modern Asian monsoon system between 27.32 and 16 Ma.

as_recorded.value: evolution of the Asian monsoon during 26–16 Ma

where.modern_name: Nyima County, Nagqu, Tibet Autonomous Region, China (proxy pin for Nima and Lunpola basins; monsoon process regional)
where.historical_name: Central Tibetan Plateau, Nima and Lunpola paleolakes; no polities existed

paleo.not_applicable: Cenozoic atmospheric monsoon circulation system spanning South Asia, the Tibetan Plateau, and East Asia.

importance.justification: The Asian monsoon system governs seasonal precipitation across South and East Asia, driving major river discharge, agricultural productivity, and continental weathering.

related.because: The collision of the Indian Plate with Eurasia drove the tectonic uplift of the Tibetan Plateau, generating the thermal and mechanical forcing for the modern monsoon.

reviewer_note: When the modern monsoon began is debated; this outline covers two studies from Tibet. The pin in Tibet marks that region, while the monsoon spans South and East Asia.
